summary: A landlocked country in southern Africa named after the medieval stone ruins of "Great Zimbabwe"; it became independent from British rule in 1980 and has Victoria Falls.

ranking.name: Apostolic churches
ranking.description: The Apostolic Church of Africa was founded in 1932 by Johane Maranke in Manicaland in the east; its members wear white robes and meet outdoors, stressing prophets, healing by the Holy Spirit and observance of Old Testament commandments. Such African-led churches blended in traditional customs such as polygamy and were closer to local culture than Western mission churches; they expanded rapidly both in the colonial period and after independence, becoming the largest religious group in Zimbabwe.

ranking.name: Pentecostalism
ranking.description: The Pentecostal "Apostolic Faith Mission" arrived from South Africa in the early 20th century, followed by indigenous Pentecostal churches such as the Zimbabwe Assemblies of God Africa, founded by Ezekiel Guti in 1960. In the 2000s, when Zimbabwe fell into a severe economic crisis and hyperinflation, large charismatic churches stressing miracles and the "prosperity gospel" attracted many city dwellers, and Pentecostalism grew rapidly.

ranking.name: Other Protestants
ranking.description: In 1859 the London Missionary Society established the first mission station at Inyati in the Ndebele Kingdom. After the British South Africa Company's occupation in 1890, Methodists, Anglicans, the Dutch Reformed Church, Lutherans and others set up mission stations and schools, training many later nationalist leaders, so other Protestant denominations still have considerable influence.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Those with no religion are mostly in cities, and some have gradually drifted from religion through modern education in the colonial period and after independence. In addition, many people mainly practice traditional beliefs such as ancestor veneration and did not register any religion in surveys, so this share also includes some followers of traditional belief.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: The Jesuits of the Catholic Church formed the Zambezi Mission and entered the area in 1879, and in 1892 established the Chishawasha mission near Harare. The former president Mugabe was educated at the Kutama Catholic mission school. In the 1980s the Catholic Commission for Justice and Peace documented the government's massacres in Matabeleland, giving the church an important place on human-rights issues.

religion.background: The Shona and Ndebele of Zimbabwe have traditionally believed in ancestral spirits and the supreme god "Mwari"; spirit mediums hold an important place in society and politics, and in the 1896-1897 uprising against the British, the spirit mediums Nehanda and Kaguvi played leading roles. Missionaries arrived from 1859, and after the British South Africa Company's occupation in 1890 churches set up schools widely. In the 20th century, apostolic and Pentecostal churches founded autonomously by Africans expanded rapidly. Today most people are Christians, but traditional rituals such as ancestor veneration remain widespread.

language.official: The constitution recognizes 16 official languages, of which English, Shona and Ndebele are most widely used.

ranking.name: Shona
ranking.description: Shona belongs to the Bantu family and is the language of the Shona, Zimbabwe's most numerous people; the people who built the Great Zimbabwe ruins in the 11th-15th centuries are generally thought to be the ancestors of the Shona. Shona originally had several dialects such as Zezuru, Karanga and Manyika, and in 1931 the linguist Clement Doke recommended merging them into a unified standard Shona. The Shona make up about 70 percent of the country, so Shona is the most widely spoken language.

ranking.name: Ndebele
ranking.description: In the 1820s-1830s Mzilikazi led his followers north from the Zulu Kingdom and about 1840 founded the Ndebele Kingdom around present-day Bulawayo, bringing the Ndebele language, which is close to Zulu. The Ndebele live mainly in Matabeleland in the southwest, and the "Gukurahundi" massacres carried out there by government forces in 1983-1987 remain a sensitive historical wound.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English became the language of administration and education after the British South Africa Company's occupation in 1890 and the founding of the colony of Southern Rhodesia. After independence in 1980 English remained the main language of government, the courts, commerce and schools, and Zimbabweans' English proficiency ranks among the highest in Africa, but those with English as a mother tongue are mainly a small number of white and urban families.

language.history: The languages of Zimbabwe mostly belong to the Bantu family, with Shona the largest; in the 19th century the northward migration of the Ndebele brought Ndebele, of the Nguni branch. Missionaries in the late 19th century devised writing systems for Shona and Ndebele, and in 1931 a unified Shona standard was set. English was the sole official language in the colonial period, and the new 2013 constitution recognizes 16 official languages, including sign language, to reflect the nation's diverse peoples.

ranking.name: Sadza
ranking.description: A thick maize porridge made by boiling white maize flour in water while stirring, formed into small balls and eaten by hand dipped in stew, greens or sour milk; it is the everyday staple of Zimbabweans.
ranking.history: Traditionally Zimbabweans made sadza from millet and sorghum; although maize was brought to Africa by the Portuguese after the 16th century, it became the main food only in the colonial period through promotion on white-owned farms and in mining areas. Zimbabweans often say that "not having eaten sadza is the same as not having eaten," and it appears at almost every meal. When the land reform and drought of the 2000s caused maize crop failures, the supply of sadza also became an important indicator of national food security.

ranking.name: Mopane worms (madora)
ranking.description: Large caterpillars collected from mopane trees are gutted, boiled and dried; they can be eaten directly as a snack or stewed with tomatoes and onions, and are rich in protein.
ranking.history: Mopane worms are the larvae of the emperor moth, living in the mopane woodlands of southern and western Zimbabwe and appearing in large numbers in the rainy season from November to January. The tradition of collecting caterpillars among southern African peoples has lasted for hundreds of years, and once dried they keep for months, making them an important source of protein. Today they are not only eaten in the countryside but also sold in city markets and even exported to neighboring countries.

ranking.name: Kapenta (dried small fish)
ranking.description: Small freshwater sardines are dried and then fried or stewed with tomatoes, onions and oil; they taste crisp and slightly salty and are one of the most common accompaniments to sadza.
ranking.history: The Kariba Dam was completed in 1959, forming one of the largest man-made lakes in the world, and in the 1960s kapenta were introduced from Lake Tanganyika, multiplying greatly in the lake and developing into an important fishery. Fishing boats on Lake Kariba attract schools of fish with lights at night, and the catch is dried and sold across the country. Because it is cheap and easy to keep, kapenta has become one of the most common sources of protein for urban and rural households in Zimbabwe.

ranking.name: Biltong
ranking.description: Beef or game such as antelope is cut into long strips, cured with salt, vinegar and spices and air-dried, making a chewy dried meat that keeps for a long time.
ranking.history: The method of making biltong came into Rhodesia with white settlers moving north from South Africa in the late 19th century, who continued the Boer tradition of curing meat with vinegar and spices. Zimbabwe's well-developed livestock industry and rich wildlife resources have made beef biltong and game biltong common snacks. Today it is common in supermarkets, gas stations and markets, and is also a convenient food for long journeys.

ranking.name: Bota (maize porridge)
ranking.description: A thinner porridge made by boiling maize meal in water, often flavored with peanut butter, sugar or milk, with a smooth, mild taste; it is a common breakfast in Zimbabwean households.
ranking.history: After maize became Zimbabwe's main staple in the colonial period, family breakfasts also came to center on maize porridge. Compared with the firm sadza, bota is thinner and easier to digest, suitable for children and for mornings. Adding peanut butter is a common practice in Zimbabwe; peanuts arrived in Africa after the 16th century and are still an important crop, and this simple bowl of porridge also carries many Zimbabweans' childhood memories.
